title: Suprascapular nerve entrapment
text: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch under the superior transverse scapular ligament (supplying supraspinatus and infraspinatus) and then around the spinoglenoid notch (infraspinatus only). Entrapment at the notch, or a paralabral ganglion cyst from a SLAP tear, weakens abduction and external rotation with wasting of the scapular fossae. Isolated infraspinatus wasting in volleyball players and overhead athletes points to compression at the spinoglenoid notch.

title: Subscapularis tear
text: The only rotator cuff muscle on the anterior scapula and the main internal rotator; tears follow anterior dislocation in older patients or forced external rotation. Tested by the lift-off test (cannot lift the hand off the lower back) and belly-press test. Tears allow the long head of biceps to dislocate medially out of the intertubercular groove.

title: Supracondylar injury and the cubital fossa
text:
The brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa, protected from the median cubital vein by the bicipital aponeurosis; venepuncture here rarely injures it, but inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes severe distal ischaemia. The artery is where blood pressure is auscultated.
Displaced supracondylar fractures kink or tear the artery: a pale, pulseless hand needs urgent reduction. Untreated forearm ischaemia leads to Volkmann ischaemic contracture of the flexor muscles.

title: Allen test, arterial lines and radial access
text:
The radial artery at the wrist, lateral to flexor carpi radialis, is the standard site for arterial blood gases, arterial lines and transradial coronary angiography. The modified Allen test checks that the ulnar artery and palmar arches can perfuse the hand if the radial artery thromboses. The radial artery is also harvested as a coronary bypass conduit.
Hypothenar hammer syndrome: repeated trauma to the ulnar artery in Guyon's canal (using the palm as a hammer) causes aneurysm or thrombosis with digital ischaemia of the ulnar fingers.

title: Subclavian steal and subclavian lines
text:
Stenosis of the proximal left subclavian artery before the vertebral artery origin makes arm exercise reverse flow down the vertebral artery, 'stealing' blood from the brain: vertigo, syncope, arm claudication and a blood pressure difference over 15 mmHg between arms.
The subclavian vein, running over the first rib in front of scalenus anterior, is used for central venous catheters because it stays open in shock; the main hazards are pneumothorax (the pleural apex lies just behind) and inadvertent arterial puncture, which cannot be compressed.

title: Axillary vessel injury
text:
The axillary artery is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor. It can be injured in anterior shoulder dislocation in the elderly (atherosclerotic, less mobile vessels), proximal humeral fractures and crutch misuse. The rich scapular anastomosis around the scapula (suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries from the subclavian with the subscapular artery) keeps the arm alive if the artery is tied off between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular branch.
Axillary vein thrombosis (effort thrombosis) follows repetitive overhead activity.

title: Scapular fractures and snapping scapula
text:
The scapula is embedded in thick muscle, so fractures signal high-energy trauma; over 80% have associated injuries such as rib fractures, pneumothorax, pulmonary contusion or brachial plexus injury. Glenoid neck fractures combined with a clavicle fracture create a 'floating shoulder'. Os acromiale, an unfused acromial ossification centre, can cause impingement.
Scapulothoracic crepitus ('snapping scapula') results from bursitis or an osteochondroma on the ventral surface.

title: Hyoid fracture in strangulation
text: Fracture of the greater horns of the hyoid is a classic forensic sign of manual strangulation, particularly in older people whose hyoid has ossified and fused; in young people the flexible hyoid may not break. The hyoid moves upward on swallowing along with thyroglossal duct cysts, and it is removed in part (Sistrunk procedure) when excising such cysts because the duct passes through or near its body.

title: Glossopharyngeal lesions and the carotid sinus
text: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex, taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, and the carotid sinus and body afferents (via the sinus nerve of Hering). Isolated lesions are rare and cause loss of the gag reflex on that side. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia produces stabbing throat and ear pain on swallowing, occasionally with syncope from reflex bradycardia. Its lesser petrosal fibres supply the parotid via the otic ganglion.

title: Tennis leg and the calf muscle pump
text:
Tennis leg: a tear of the medial head of gastrocnemius at the musculotendinous junction during push-off, causing sudden calf pain as if struck, bruising and swelling; it must be distinguished from DVT and Achilles rupture.
Soleus and gastrocnemius form the calf muscle pump that drives venous return through the deep veins; immobility (long flights, surgery, plaster casts) stops this pump and predisposes to deep venous thrombosis within the soleal venous sinuses. Soleus is sometimes called the 'second heart'.

title: Hamstring and rectus femoris strains and avulsions
text:
The two-joint muscles are the most frequently strained, because they are stretched across both hip and knee during sprinting and kicking. Hamstring injuries usually involve the long head of biceps femoris at the musculotendinous junction; complete proximal avulsion from the ischial tuberosity (water-skiing, forced hip flexion with knee extension) needs early surgical repair and can involve the sciatic nerve nearby.
In adolescents, apophyseal avulsions occur at the ischial tuberosity (hamstrings), anterior inferior iliac spine (rectus femoris) and anterior superior iliac spine (sartorius).

title: Anterior compartment syndrome and shin splints
text:
The anterior compartment of the leg is tightly bound by tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and crural fascia. Exertional compartment syndrome in runners causes predictable anterolateral pain that resolves with rest; acute compartment syndrome after tibial fracture threatens the deep fibular nerve (numbness in the first web space is an early sign) and anterior tibial artery.
Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) is traction periostitis along the posteromedial tibia at the origins of soleus and tibialis posterior.

title: Adult-acquired flatfoot
text: Tibialis posterior is the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch, inserting chiefly on the navicular tuberosity. Degeneration and rupture of its tendon behind the medial malleolus (a hypovascular zone), common in obese middle-aged women, flattens the arch, abducts the forefoot ('too many toes' sign seen from behind) and prevents a single-leg heel raise. The spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament fails subsequently.

title: Fifth metatarsal fractures and peroneal tendon injury
text:
Inversion injuries avulse the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal (pulled by fibularis brevis and the lateral band of the plantar aponeurosis), which heals well. A Jones fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction lies in a vascular watershed and is prone to non-union, often needing screw fixation in athletes.
The peroneal tendons can sublux out of the retromalleolar groove if the superior fibular retinaculum tears, giving painful snapping behind the lateral malleolus.

title: Iliotibial band syndrome
text: Friction or compression of the fat pad beneath the iliotibial tract as it passes over the lateral femoral epicondyle at about 30° of knee flexion causes lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists, worse downhill (Noble compression test). Proximally, the band can snap over the greater trochanter (external snapping hip). Weak hip abductors are a contributing factor.

title: Pectoralis major rupture, Poland syndrome and pectoralis minor
text:
Pectoralis major ruptures at its humeral insertion during bench pressing, especially with anabolic steroid use, producing bruising, a deformed anterior axillary fold and weak adduction and internal rotation.
Poland syndrome: congenital absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major with ipsilateral hand anomalies (syndactyly), attributed to subclavian artery hypoplasia in the embryo.
Pectoralis minor is the key landmark dividing the axillary artery into three parts and axillary lymph nodes into levels I-III for breast cancer surgery; a tight pectoralis minor can compress the neurovascular bundle (pectoralis minor syndrome).

title: Temporomandibular disorders and trismus
text:
Temporomandibular joint dysfunction causes jaw pain, clicking and limited opening; overactivity of the muscles of mastication (bruxism) is a common factor, with masseter hypertrophy. The lateral pterygoid pulls the articular disc and condyle forward; anterior disc displacement causes clicking and, if the disc no longer reduces, a 'closed lock'.
Trismus results from spasm of masseter or medial pterygoid in dental infection, peritonsillar abscess, tetanus (lockjaw) and tumours of the infratemporal fossa. Jaw claudication on chewing is a key symptom of giant cell arteritis.

title: Ptosis and inability to close the eye
text:
Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve, so a third nerve palsy causes complete ptosis; the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle has sympathetic supply, so Horner syndrome causes only partial ptosis. Fatigable ptosis worse at the end of the day suggests myasthenia gravis (improves with an ice pack). Age-related levator aponeurosis dehiscence is the commonest cause of ptosis in the elderly.
Orbicularis oculi is supplied by the facial nerve; facial palsy prevents eye closure, risking exposure keratopathy (Bell phenomenon shows the eye rolling up).

title: Extraocular muscle disease: thyroid eye disease and blow-out fractures
text:
Graves orbitopathy causes lymphocytic infiltration and swelling of the extraocular muscle bellies (typically inferior rectus, then medial rectus) with tendon sparing, producing proptosis, restricted up-gaze and diplopia; severe swelling at the orbital apex compresses the optic nerve.
Orbital floor fractures trap inferior rectus, preventing upward gaze and triggering the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia) in children. The rhyme 'LR6 SO4, rest 3' summarises innervation; superior oblique depresses the eye most effectively when it is adducted.

title: Aortic arch anomalies and tracheo-innominate fistula
text:
An aberrant right subclavian artery arising last from the arch passes behind the oesophagus and can compress it (dysphagia lusoria). A double aortic arch or right arch with a left ligamentum arteriosum forms a vascular ring around the trachea and oesophagus, causing stridor in infants.
The brachiocephalic trunk crosses in front of the trachea at the thoracic inlet; a low tracheostomy tube can erode into it, producing a sentinel bleed followed by massive haemorrhage (tracheo-innominate fistula).

title: Tetralogy of Fallot and pulmonary stenosis
text:
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum produces the four features of tetralogy of Fallot: right ventricular outflow obstruction (pulmonary stenosis), ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy ('boot-shaped heart'). Children have cyanotic 'tet spells' relieved by squatting, which raises systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting.
Isolated pulmonary valve stenosis gives an ejection click and systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge; it is associated with Noonan syndrome and treated by balloon valvuloplasty.

title: Coronary sinus in pacing and retroplegia
text: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy places the left ventricular pacing lead through the coronary sinus into a lateral cardiac vein. During cardiac surgery, cardioplegia can be given retrogradely through the sinus. A persistent left superior vena cava drains into and dilates the coronary sinus, and complicates line and pacemaker insertion from the left.

title: Anterior mediastinal masses in children and adults
text: In infants the normal thymus is large and can mimic a mass on chest X-ray (the 'sail sign'). Anterior mediastinal masses in young adults are mostly lymphoma (Hodgkin and T-lymphoblastic) or germ cell tumours; they may compress the trachea and cause collapse under general anaesthesia when muscle tone is lost, a critical anaesthetic hazard.

title: Gluteal injections and gluteal nerve injury
text:
Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (or ventrogluteal site between the ASIS and iliac crest) to avoid the sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels and nerve. Superior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus medius and minimus, giving a positive Trendelenburg sign.
Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve) is the powerful hip extensor for climbing stairs and rising from sitting; weakness causes a backward lurching gait.

title: Coarctation collaterals and internal thoracic artery grafts
text:
In coarctation of the aorta, blood bypasses the narrowing through the subclavian, internal thoracic and intercostal arteries; the enlarged posterior intercostal arteries erode the inferior margins of ribs 3 to 8 ('rib notching').
The left internal thoracic (mammary) artery grafted to the LAD is the gold-standard coronary bypass conduit, with over 90% patency at 10 years, much better than saphenous vein grafts. Harvesting both reduces sternal blood supply and raises the risk of sternal wound infection in diabetics.

title: Inferior epigastric artery in laparoscopy and hernias
text: The inferior epigastric artery ascends in the posterior rectus sheath from the external iliac artery and is the landmark separating direct (medial) from indirect (lateral) inguinal hernias. It can be injured by lateral laparoscopic port insertion, causing rectus sheath haematoma, so lateral ports are placed lateral to the rectus sheath under direct vision. It is also used as the pedicle for DIEP flaps in breast reconstruction.

title: Sacroiliitis
text: Inflammatory back pain from sacroiliitis (worse in the morning and at rest, improved by exercise, alternating buttock pain) is the hallmark of axial spondyloarthritis: ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthritis, all associated with HLA-B27. MRI shows bone marrow oedema before radiographic erosions and fusion. Septic sacroiliitis occurs in intravenous drug users and pregnancy.

title: Spinal stenosis and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
text:
Hypertrophy and buckling of the ligamenta flava, facet joint osteophytes and disc bulging narrow the lumbar canal, causing neurogenic claudication: bilateral leg pain and heaviness on walking or standing, relieved by sitting or leaning forward (shopping-trolley sign), with preserved pulses.
Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (commoner in East Asian populations and with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis) causes cervical myelopathy. The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow laterally, which is why discs herniate posterolaterally. A 'loss of resistance' is felt when an epidural needle passes through the ligamentum flavum.

title: Brain herniation syndromes
text:
Subfalcine herniation: the cingulate gyrus is pushed under the falx cerebri, compressing the anterior cerebral artery and causing contralateral leg weakness.
Transtentorial (uncal) herniation: the medial temporal lobe squeezes through the tentorial notch, compressing the oculomotor nerve (ipsilateral dilated pupil), the posterior cerebral artery (occipital infarction) and the cerebral peduncle. Compression of the opposite peduncle against the tentorial edge (Kernohan notch) causes a false-localising hemiparesis on the same side as the lesion. Stretching of basilar perforators causes Duret brainstem haemorrhages.
Meningiomas commonly arise along the falx and tentorium.

title: Localising visual field defects
text: Optic nerve lesion: monocular blindness. Chiasmal compression (pituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma, anterior communicating artery aneurysm): bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesion: incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Temporal optic radiation (Meyer's loop): contralateral superior quadrantanopia. Parietal radiation: inferior quadrantanopia. Occipital cortex: congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

title: Ossicular chain disruption and cholesteatoma
text:
Temporal bone fractures and blast injury can dislocate the incudostapedial joint, the weakest link in the chain, causing a large conductive hearing loss despite an intact eardrum. A cholesteatoma (keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear, often from an attic retraction pocket) erodes the long process of the incus first and can extend to the lateral semicircular canal (vertigo), facial nerve and tegmen (intracranial abscess).
Paralysis of stapedius (facial nerve) makes loud sounds painful (hyperacusis); tensor tympani is supplied by the mandibular nerve.

title: Atrial fibrillation and pulmonary vein isolation
text: Ectopic beats triggering atrial fibrillation arise most often from myocardial sleeves extending into the pulmonary veins; catheter ablation electrically isolates the pulmonary veins from the left atrium. Complications include pulmonary vein stenosis, phrenic nerve palsy during right-sided cryoablation, and atrio-oesophageal fistula because the oesophagus lies directly behind the posterior left atrial wall (also why transoesophageal echocardiography gives excellent images of the left atrium and its appendage, where thrombi form).

title: Hepatic arterial variants and hepatic vein anatomy
text:
Hepatic arterial anatomy is 'textbook' in only about half of people: a replaced or accessory right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery runs behind the pancreatic head and bile duct, and a replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric artery runs in the lesser omentum; both must be identified before liver transplant, Whipple procedure or cholecystectomy.
The three hepatic veins run between Couinaud segments and drain directly into the IVC just below the diaphragm; their thrombosis causes Budd-Chiari syndrome, and the middle hepatic vein marks the plane of right versus left hepatectomy.

title: Coeliac disease and jejunal diverticulosis
text:
Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (HLA-DQ2/DQ8, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies) causes villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis most severe in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, where iron, folate and calcium are absorbed; hence iron-deficiency anaemia and osteoporosis. Dermatitis herpetiformis is its skin manifestation; long-standing disease raises the risk of enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.
Jejunal diverticula on the mesenteric border cause bacterial overgrowth with B12 deficiency.

title: Tongue and airway obstruction
text:
Genioglossus pulls the tongue forward; when muscle tone is lost (unconsciousness, anaesthesia, sleep) the tongue falls back against the posterior pharyngeal wall, obstructing the airway. The jaw-thrust manoeuvre and oropharyngeal airways counteract this. In obstructive sleep apnoea, reduced genioglossus activity during sleep contributes to collapse, and hypoglossal nerve stimulators are an implantable treatment.
Macroglossia occurs in hypothyroidism, acromegaly, amyloidosis, Down syndrome and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

title: Palmaris longus as a tendon graft
text: Palmaris longus is absent in about 15% of people (test by opposing thumb and little finger with the wrist flexed). Because it is expendable, its tendon is the first choice for tendon grafts (e.g. ulnar collateral ligament 'Tommy John' reconstruction). It lies superficial to the flexor retinaculum, with the median nerve just deep and slightly lateral to it, which makes it a useful landmark for median nerve blocks and a reminder of the nerve's vulnerability to wrist lacerations.

title: Pes anserinus bursitis and hamstring grafts
text:
Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert together on the medial proximal tibia (pes anserinus, 'goose's foot'), over a bursa that becomes inflamed in overweight people with knee osteoarthritis and runners, causing medial knee pain below the joint line.
The gracilis and semitendinosus tendons are commonly harvested for ACL reconstruction; the saphenous nerve's infrapatellar branch can be injured during harvest, numbing the anterior knee. Gracilis is also a free flap for facial reanimation.

title: Posterolateral corner injury
text:
The fibular collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and popliteofibular ligament form the posterolateral corner of the knee, resisting varus and external rotation. Injury (varus hyperextension, dashboard impact) often accompanies cruciate tears and is frequently missed, causing reconstruction failure; the dial test shows excess external rotation. The common fibular nerve is injured in about a third of cases.
Popliteus 'unlocks' the extended knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia at the start of flexion.

title: Hiccups, referred pain and the oesophageal hiatus
text:
The oesophagus passes through a sling of the right crus at T10; the crura act as an external lower oesophageal sphincter, and a widened hiatus allows hiatus hernia. Persistent hiccups (involuntary diaphragmatic contraction) can signal irritation along the phrenic or vagus nerves: mediastinal tumours, subphrenic abscess, uraemia, or brainstem lesions.
Irritation of the peripheral diaphragm refers pain to the lower thoracic wall (intercostal nerves), while central diaphragm irritation refers to the shoulder tip (C4).
